title: Copy one array into another array.
shortTitle: Copy one array into another array
keyPoints: Copying creates a new array of the same length and places each source element into the corresponding destination position.
Java offers four approaches: manual loop, System.arraycopy, Arrays.copyOf, and clone().
All four produce a shallow copy for object arrays, meaning references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared.
Shallow copy is safe for immutable types like BigDecimal because the shared objects cannot be modified.
For mutable element types a deep copy is needed to make the arrays truly independent.
Time is O(n) and space is O(n) for the new array, regardless of which approach is used.

s1_definition.oneliner: Make a fresh array of the same size and place each element into it; for objects this copies references, not the objects themselves.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **New array** – allocate a destination array of the same length as the source.
- **Element copy** – place each source element into the corresponding destination position.
- **Shallow copy** – for object arrays, references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared.
- **Built-in methods** – `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, and `clone()` all perform shallow copies.
- **O(n) time and O(n) space** – every copy must touch each element once and allocate a new array.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to archive Rajesh's current transaction list before running a risky interest recalculation. A clerk photocopies the whole list onto a fresh sheet so the original is safe. If the recalculation goes wrong, the archived copy is untouched and can be restored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Copying an array means creating a brand new array of the same length and placing each source element into the matching position of the destination. In Java I can do this with a simple loop, or with built-in helpers like System.arraycopy, Arrays.copyOf, or the clone method. All run in linear time and allocate a destination of the same size.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used array copying to take a backup before a risky interest recalculation. Before the batch job overwrites Rajesh's transaction amounts, I copy the original list into an archive array, so if the recalculation produces wrong figures I can roll back to the archived copy.

The subtle point I always raise is shallow versus deep copy. For an array of objects, these copy operations duplicate the references, not the objects themselves, so both arrays point at the same underlying objects. In my case the elements are BigDecimal, which is immutable, so a shallow copy is completely safe. If the elements had been mutable objects, I would need a deep copy that clones each element individually.

Remember one sentence: all Java array copy methods produce a shallow copy, which is safe for immutable types like BigDecimal but requires deep cloning for mutable elements.
